description_full: Tesla, Inc. designs, develops, manufactures, leases, and sells electric vehicles, and energy generation and storage systems in the United States, China, and internationally. The company operates in two segments, Automotive; and Energy Generation and Storage. The company offers electric vehicles, as well as sells automotive regulatory credits; and non-warranty maintenance services and collision, automotive insurance services, as well as part sales and retail merchandise sale. It also provides sedans and sport utility vehicles through direct and used vehicle sales, a network of Tesla Superchargers, and in-app upgrades; purchase financing and leasing services; services for electric vehicles through its company-owned service locations and Tesla mobile service technicians; and vehicle limited warranties and extended service plans. In addition, the company engages in the design, manufacture, installation, sale, and leasing of solar energy generation and energy storage products, and related services to residential, commercial, and industrial customers and utilities through its website, stores, and galleries, as well as through a network of channel partners. Further, it provides services and repairs to its energy product customers, including under warranty and extended service plans; and various financing options to its residential customers; lithium-ion battery energy storage products, such as Powerwall and Megapack; energy generation products, including solar panels and solar roof; self-driving development and artificial intelligence software, vehicle control and infotainment software, and battery and powertrain. The company was formerly known as Tesla Motors, Inc. and changed its name to Tesla, Inc. in February 2017. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in 2003 and is headquartered in Austin, Texas.

financial_summary: Tesla, Inc. is a mega-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.4T market cap on $94.8B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +37% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +9.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at 30% against a 12% cost of capital — a 18-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 21% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $6.2B in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.89× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 15% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 8% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 28% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $37.65 (margin of safety -851%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 31%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $25.01 to $61.25 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 393.6 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 135.2 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 227.6 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 42% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 40 covering analysts target $413 on average, 15% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 30% clears the cost of capital of 12.0% by 18pp, the mark of a value creator.
It runs a 21% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.89x.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 6.8% of revenue on R&D and 3.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $37.5B (3% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 17.0, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.2% over 3 years, 24.6% over 5 years and 37.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 93%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 29.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 17.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.03, a backlog worth 11% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 9%.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (9.0% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders own 17.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 44%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (66 sales, net $87.7M sold).
The share count has grown 5.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 134,785 employees, each generates about $704K of revenue, 1.9x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 55.1% a year.
That works out to $46K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
Compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
